front: What was the "stab in the back" myth?
back: The false claim that Germany's army hadn't really been defeated, but betrayed by politicians at home — fed resentment toward the new republic.
Hyperinflation (savings became worthless) combined with French occupation of the Ruhr after Germany defaulted on reparations.

front: Name two things Stresemann did to help Germany recover.
back: Any two of: introduced the Rentenmark, negotiated the Dawes Plan and Young Plan, signed the Locarno Pact, joined the League of Nations.
Hitler's failed attempt to seize power by force — led to his trial, imprisonment, and writing Mein Kampf; he shifted toward gaining power legally afterward.

front: How did Hitler become Chancellor in January 1933?
back: Through backroom dealing — Hindenburg and von Papen believed they could control him by bringing him into government.

front: What did the Enabling Act (March 1933) do?
back: Let Hitler pass laws without the Reichstag, effectively ending democracy in Germany.

front: What was the Night of the Long Knives (1934)?
back: Hitler eliminated Röhm and other SA/rival figures who were seen as a threat to his power.

front: What happened after Hindenburg's death in August 1934?
back: Hitler merged the roles of Chancellor and President into "Führer", and the army swore a personal oath of loyalty to him.
Laws that stripped Jewish people of German citizenship rights — a major step in Nazi persecution of Jews.
A coordinated, violent pogrom against Jewish people and businesses — a major escalation in Nazi persecution.

front: What was the Hitler Youth / League of German Maidens for?
back: Indoctrinating young people into Nazi ideology, alongside tight control of education.
